title: Congo Bans Copper and Cobalt Concentrate Exports to Force Domestic Processing
excerpt: The world's largest cobalt producer and a major copper source escalates its push to retain mineral wealth, sending London copper prices to near-record highs.
body:
• The Democratic Republic of Congo has banned exports of copper and cobalt concentrates, effective immediately, to force domestic processing
  • Benchmark London copper rose 1.8% to $14,369.50 per metric ton after Reuters reported the ban — near the all-time high of $14,527.50
  • One-year export waivers may be granted under "strategic circumstances," and Ivanhoe Mines says its Kamoa-Kakula complex has existing exemptions
  • The ban builds on Congo's earlier four-month cobalt export suspension and signals a broader strategy to capture more value from critical minerals

The Ban

The Democratic Republic of Congo has banned exports of copper and cobalt concentrates as it escalates efforts to force domestic processing and retain more value from its mineral resources, according to a government order reviewed by Reuters on Thursday.

The June 29 order, signed by Mines Minister Louis Kabamba Watum, Foreign Trade Minister Julien Paluku Kahongya, and Economy Minister Daniel Mukoko Samba, states plainly: "The export of copper and cobalt concentrates is prohibited."

The ban takes effect immediately, although one-year export waivers may be granted under strategic circumstances, the order said, without elaborating. It also introduced a tax regime with a three-month transition period for economically significant mining by-products.

Market Reaction

After Reuters reported the ban, benchmark three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange rose as much as 1.8% to $14,369.50 a metric ton — the highest since January 29, when the metal hit an all-time peak of $14,527.50.

The price move reflects the market's sensitivity to any supply disruption from Congo, which is the world's largest cobalt producer and Africa's biggest copper source. Cobalt is essential for lithium-ion batteries used in electric vehicles, while copper is critical for electrical wiring, renewable energy infrastructure, and data centers.

Who Is Affected

Major producers with existing processing capacity in Congo are likely to be less affected. Ivanhoe Mines said in a statement on Thursday that its Kamoa-Kakula copper complex — a joint venture with China's Zijin Mining and the Congolese government — had received multiple exemptions allowing it to export copper concentrate since production began in 2021.

Copper concentrate produced at Kamoa-Kakula is currently smelted at an on-site smelter or at the Lualaba copper smelter in Kolwezi, the company said. Its Kipushi Mine also has a derogation allowing zinc concentrate exports.

Chinese mining operators, however, face greater exposure. Chinese firms dominate cobalt mining in Congo, and some have faced allegations that their cobalt contains excessive uranium levels — claims the companies have denied.

A Pattern of Resource Nationalism

The ban is the latest in a series of moves by Kinshasa to leverage its mineral wealth. Congo halted cobalt exports entirely for four months beginning in February 2025 to address a global supply glut that had driven prices to nine-year lows. That suspension pushed cobalt prices up more than 50%, according to government data.

Congo has also signaled intentions to impose export quotas on cobalt and partner with Indonesia, another major producer, to manage pricing and supply — echoing the cartel-style approach OPEC has used for oil.

The country has technically banned concentrate exports since 2013, but routinely granted waivers. The new order appears to tighten enforcement significantly, though the waiver mechanism remains in place.

Implications for India and Global Supply Chains

India's rapidly growing electric vehicle battery industry and electronics manufacturing sector depend heavily on stable cobalt and copper supply chains. Any sustained disruption in Congolese exports could drive up input costs for Indian manufacturers and delay the country's EV transition timeline.

For global markets, the ban adds another layer of uncertainty to critical mineral supply chains already strained by geopolitical competition between the U.S. and China for access to Congo's resources. Washington has been pushing for greater access to Congolese minerals as part of its broader effort to reduce dependence on Chinese-controlled supply chains.

What to Watch

The key question is enforcement. Congo's previous concentrate export bans were widely circumvented through waivers. Whether Kinshasa follows through more aggressively this time — and whether major mining companies seek new exemptions — will determine the ban's real impact on global copper and cobalt markets.
